primary_sources: J. Allen St. John, "The Hun—his Mark. Blot it Out with Liberty Bonds" poster, ca. 1917

stimulus.text: The poster shows a large red handprint, like a bloody hand pressed to the page. Below it, large lettering reads: "The Hun—his Mark / Blot it Out / with / LIBERTY BONDS." The poster was drawn by J. Allen St. John in about 1917.
stimulus.source_note: Poster by J. Allen St. John, ca. 1917, U.S. Food Administration (NARA 512466), public domain.

source: original; stimulus image from the shared pool, J. Allen St. John poster, ca. 1917, public domain
stem: The poster's appeal to ordinary Americans to fund the war is most similar to which later wartime practice?

options.text: the sale of war bonds to the public during World War II
the federal rationing of gasoline and rubber in World War II
options.misconception: Rationing limited what families could buy; it did not ask them to lend money to the government.

options.text: the internment of Japanese Americans during World War II
options.misconception: Internment removed people from their homes; it had nothing to do with funding the war.

options.text: the use of the draft to raise an army in the Korean War
options.misconception: The draft raised soldiers, not money; the poster asks for money, not men.

rationales.A: In both wars the government sold bonds to ordinary Americans so the public, not just taxes, would pay for the fighting.
rationales.B: Rationing limited what families could buy. It did not ask them to lend money to the government.
rationales.C: Internment removed people from their homes. It had nothing to do with funding the war.
rationales.D: The draft raised soldiers, not money. The poster asks for money, not men.
rationales.general:
1. Name what the poster asks for: money from ordinary people, lent to the government.
2. Ask which later practice asked for the same thing. War bond drives did; rationing, internment, and the draft did not.
3. Match the kind of action, not just the wartime setting.
Remember: to compare practices across wars, match what each one asked people to do.
